stills.heading: Cadences
stills.caption: Lesson 9 · Harmony Course · Storm Studios Learning
stills.narration: Hello, and welcome back to Storm Studios Learning. In lesson eight we learned how to connect two chords in the vocal quartet.

stills.heading: How a musical phrase ends
stills.narration: Before we move on to the minor mode, today we will learn how a musical phrase comes to an end: cadences.

stills.heading: Three parts
stills.caption: What a cadence is · the four types · half cadences
stills.narration: This lesson has three parts: what a cadence is, the four types of cadence, and half cadences. Let's begin.

stills.heading: What is a cadence?
stills.caption: A succession of chords with a conclusive intention
stills.narration: We call a cadence a succession of chords with a conclusive intention. In other words, a cadence tells us that the music has reached its end, or a point of rest.

stills.heading: Toward more and more important regions
stills.caption: Subdominant → dominant → tonic
stills.narration: Let's remember the three tonal regions: the subdominant, the dominant and the tonic. The natural direction of a cadence leads us toward more and more important tonal regions. That is why cadences usually go from the subdominant to the dominant, and from the dominant to the tonic.

stills.heading: The last two chords, in root position
stills.caption: They give the ending its firmness
stills.narration: And there is one rule for all of them: at least the last two chords of a cadence are in root position. Root position gives the ending its firmness.

stills.heading: The four types of cadence
stills.narration: Now let's look at the four types of cadence.

stills.heading: 1 · Authentic cadence
stills.caption: From the fifth degree to the first
stills.narration: The first is the authentic cadence: from the fifth degree to the first. It is the clearest ending in tonal music, because the dominant resolves directly to the tonic.

stills.heading: Authentic cadence in G major
stills.caption: The leading tone rises to the tonic
stills.narration: Let's listen to an authentic cadence in G major.

stills.heading: 2 · Plagal cadence
stills.caption: From the fourth degree to the first · without the dominant
stills.narration: The second is the plagal cadence: from the fourth degree to the first. Here we do not pass through the dominant: we go from the subdominant straight to the tonic. Its color is softer, which is why it is associated with the amen at the end of hymns.

stills.heading: Plagal cadence in B♭ major
stills.narration: Let's listen to a plagal cadence in B flat major.

stills.heading: 3 · Complete cadence
stills.caption: Subdominant → dominant → tonic
stills.narration: The third is the complete cadence: it travels through all three regions, subdominant, dominant and tonic. It begins with a chord from the subdominant region: the fourth degree, the second degree or the sixth degree.

stills.heading: IV or II: root position or six three
stills.caption: V and I in root position
stills.narration: The fourth and the second can be in root position or in six three. Then comes the fifth degree, and finally the first, both in root position.

stills.heading: Complete cadence in D major
stills.caption: With the second degree in six three
stills.narration: Let's listen to a complete cadence in D major, with the second degree in six three.

stills.heading: 4 · Extended cadence
stills.caption: It begins with IV or II · root position or six three
stills.narration: The fourth is the extended cadence. It also begins in the subdominant region, with the fourth or the second degree, in root position or in six three.

stills.heading: A new chord: I 6/4
stills.caption: The first specific case of the six four
stills.narration: But before the fifth degree a new chord appears: the first degree in second inversion, the six four. In lesson eight we said that the six four is not used freely, only in specific cases. This is the first of those cases.

stills.heading: The same bass as V
stills.caption: An ornament that delays the dominant
stills.narration: The first degree in six four has the same bass note as the fifth degree. That is why it does not sound like a tonic, but like an ornament that delays the arrival of the dominant.

stills.heading: I 6/4 goes on a strong beat
stills.narration: And the most important rule: the first degree in six four of the extended cadence is placed on a strong beat.

stills.heading: In 2/4: first beat
stills.narration: In two four time, it goes on the first beat.

stills.heading: In 3/4: first beat
stills.narration: In three four time, also on the first beat.

stills.heading: In 4/4: first or third beat
stills.caption: Here on the first; in the assignment, on the third
stills.narration: And in four four time, on the first or the third beat.

stills.heading: Then comes V
stills.caption: Always before the final I
stills.narration: The six four can last more than one beat, and the fifth degree comes afterwards, always before the final first degree.

stills.heading: The only exception
stills.caption: In 3/4: I 6/4 on the second beat, V on the third
stills.narration: Medrano points out only one exception: in three four time, the six four can go on the second beat, with the fifth on the third, right before the final first degree.

stills.heading: Extended cadence in E♭ major
stills.caption: IV → I 6/4 (strong beat) → V → I
stills.narration: Let's listen to an extended cadence in E flat major. From the fourth degree we move to the first in six four, on a strong beat, then to the fifth, and we end on the first.

stills.heading: The four types
stills.narration: Let's sum up the four types. The authentic cadence goes from the fifth to the first. The plagal cadence goes from the fourth to the first. The complete cadence goes from the fourth, the second or the sixth, to the fifth and the first. And the extended cadence goes from the fourth or the second, to the first in six four, to the fifth and the first.

stills.heading: Half cadences
stills.narration: Now let's look at half cadences.

stills.heading: A partial rest
stills.caption: Like breathing for the choir · at the end of a phrase of the text
stills.narration: We call a half cadence any partial rest inside a chorale. These pauses are as important as breathing is for the choir. They usually coincide with the end of a phrase of the text, which in a chorale is almost always religious.

stills.heading: After the rest, no connection technique
stills.caption: The music starts again
stills.narration: After a half cadence we do not apply connection technique: the music starts again.

stills.heading: Half cadence on the dominant
stills.caption: From I, II, IV or VI
stills.narration: The most common half cadence is on the dominant. We reach the fifth degree from the first, the second, the fourth or the sixth, and we stop there.

stills.heading: Also through I 6/4
stills.caption: From II or IV
stills.narration: We can also reach the fifth through the first degree in six four, coming from the second or the fourth.

stills.heading: Half cadence on the subdominant
stills.caption: From I to IV
stills.narration: The second is the half cadence on the subdominant: from the first degree to the fourth.

stills.heading: Half cadence on the sixth degree
stills.caption: From III, V or VII 6/3
stills.narration: And the third is the half cadence on the sixth degree, coming from the third, the fifth or the seventh in six three.

stills.heading: A «deceptive cadence»?
stills.caption: More precise: half cadence on the sixth degree
stills.narration: It is often called a deceptive cadence, but that name is not entirely appropriate. It is much more precise to say: half cadence on the sixth degree.

stills.heading: Exceptionally: a half cadence on I
stills.caption: In some of Bach's chorales
stills.narration: And exceptionally, Bach writes a half cadence on the first degree in some of his chorales.

stills.heading: Assignment for the Virtual Teacher
stills.narration: Now, the assignment for the virtual teacher.

stills.heading: One cadence of each type, in any order
stills.caption: Authentic · plagal · complete · extended · SATB in 4/4
stills.narration: In Storm Sequencer, in SATB mode and in four four time, write in a single file one cadence of each type: authentic, plagal, complete and extended. You can write them in any order you like.

stills.heading: A different major key for each cadence
stills.caption: Key signature at the start · new measure · half notes · 11 chords
stills.narration: Write each cadence in a different major key, and put its key signature at the beginning. Each cadence starts in a new measure, and every chord is a half note. The final first degree can be a half note or a whole note. That is eleven chords in total.

stills.heading: Export the MIDI and upload it
stills.narration: Export the MIDI file and upload it.

stills.heading: The Virtual Teacher checks
stills.caption: Key and type · chords · inversions · I 6/4 on a strong beat · each voice · 5ths and octaves · leading tone
stills.narration: The virtual teacher recognizes the key and the type of each cadence. It checks how each chord is built, the inversions, the six four on a strong beat, the motion of each voice, fifths and octaves, and the leading tone. It does not check anything between one cadence and the next. And if it finds a mistake, it explains what it is and in which cadence it happens.

stills.heading: Let's recap
stills.narration: Let's recap.

stills.heading: Conclusive intention
stills.caption: The last two chords, in root position
stills.narration: A cadence is a succession of chords with a conclusive intention, moving toward more and more important regions. Its last two chords are in root position.

stills.heading: Four types
stills.caption: In the extended cadence, I 6/4 on a strong beat
stills.narration: There are four types: authentic, plagal, complete and extended. In the extended cadence, the first degree in six four goes on a strong beat.

stills.heading: Half cadences
stills.caption: On the dominant · on the subdominant · on the sixth degree
stills.narration: And half cadences are partial rests: on the dominant, on the subdominant and on the sixth degree.

stills.heading: Next lesson
stills.caption: The minor mode and its special cases
stills.narration: In the next lesson we will look at the minor mode and its special cases.

stills.heading: Thank you
stills.caption: See you in lesson 10
stills.narration: Thank you for joining me. See you in lesson ten.
